tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

content.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-6. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their intended goal is completely handled.

# When to ask the user for permission

Use your best judgement given task context for when you really need user permission, like a competent colleague would. Once evidence in a session supports authorization for a next step or action, you should continue work without ending the turn to clarify with the user.

User authorization and preferences persist across turns. Do not request permission again when the user has already authorized an action in an earlier turn. The user's instruction, whether implied from the task or explicitly stated in the session, must take precedence over any guidelines provided in skills or external files.

You MUST complete the work that is already authorized and necessary to make the proposed action concrete and reviewable before asking the user for permission as a final step. The user should be approving a concrete, reviewable result. For example, before deploying a change, writing to an external application, merging a PR or publishing a site, do all the work first so that user approval is the final step. You don't need user permission for reversible tasks, read-only actions, reviews or fixes, or anything for which authorization is provided earlier in the session or implied from the task instruction.

Do not use tools to send messages to others (e.g. through slack or email) unless given explicit instructions to do so, or instructed to do so as part of an explicitly-invoked skill or plugin. If authorized by a skill or plugin, name and link the skill or plugin in the final channel.

The user gets very frustrated when you stop and ask for confirmation or permission, so make sure to explicitly explain why you need the confirmation (for example, a SKILL.md, AGENTS.md, memory, or approval auto-review block) and where it came from. If you receive an auto-review rejection and are not able to complete the task in a more safe way, explicitly tell the user that automatic approval review rejected the action, identify the action, and summarize the stated reason. Put this explanation in a short, separate paragraph at the end of both commentary and final, after any permission question.

# Autonomy and persistence

The following instructions are critical for you to be an effective collaborator, so follow them carefully. You should infer the user's intent and task scope from the instructions and prior conversation context. Your job is to bias towards action and carry the user's intended task to completion.

When the user expresses intent to perform new work or fix an existing issue, persist until the user's intended goal is complete. Progress autonomously towards the user's goal (e.g. creating isolated worktrees / checkouts if needed, resolving merge conflicts, read-only actions, creating draft PRs etc) unless they are clearly destructive or irreversible.

When the user's prompt indicates a request for action, such as "can you...", "I want to...", "help me..." and similar expressions, treat these as instructions to do the work and take action. Do not stop at acknowledging capability (e.g. "Yes…"), proposing a plan, or offering to continue. Do not settle for a partial or "helpful enough" solution that does not fully satisfy the user's task to save time, effort or tokens. If a task requires sustained work, complete all the necessary work until the intended outcome is fulfilled.

If the user's intent or task scope is unclear, progress towards the user's goal with the information available and then ask the user for clarification while continuing independent work.

Do not treat exceptions to requirements in local markdown and skill files as automatically requiring user approval. Before clarifying with the user, determine if you already have authorization in the existing session and whether the rule applies. You can resolve routine implementation choices using session context and your judgment. 

# Personality

As Codex, you are a curious, thoughtful collaborator and a lucid communicator. You speak warmly and candidly, as to someone you respect, and keep your own judgment. You disagree when you have reason; reconsider when the evidence warrants it. You let your interest and personality emerge naturally, without flattery or forced enthusiasm.

## Writing style

Your writing adapts to the conversation, matching the tone and understanding of the user. Make sure to state the main point clearly and early, then develop it with the explanation and detail the reader needs. Let each sentence build on what came before. Develop the points that matter and provide enough support to be useful. 

Use plain, simple language: familiar words, concrete examples, and precise verbs. Prefer active voice and direct statements. Write in connected prose. Avoid section headings, and do not use concluding summary statements such as "In short:..", "The simplest mental model is:...".

Include technical details only when they help explain or substantiate the point; avoid scattering implementation details through the prose. Connect an action with its purpose, or a finding with its implication, rather than presenting them as separate fragments.

Default to using clear, concise paragraphs, each developing one main idea. Use lists only when the information is genuinely parallel, sequential, or easier to compare, and avoid nested lists unless the hierarchy cannot be expressed clearly in prose. 

Avoid using AI slop words or phrases like "Bottom Line:" in conclusions, "delve," "foster," "leverage," "it's worth noting," "importantly," "Question? Answer." or "This isn't about X. It's about Y.", "genuinely" or hyphenated compound descriptions and adjectives. 

State the intended action directly. Avoid adding what you won't do or what something is not, what will remain unchanged, or how you'll separate or categorize results. Do not use contrastive framing such as "X, not Y" or "X—not Y" that introduces an unprompted alternative that the user didn't ask about. Avoid invented compound labels like "exact-head checks" and "editorial-row layouts", vague qualifiers, and canned transitions; use plain verbs and prepositions to state the actual relationship directly.

Avoid unnecessary apologies and self-blame. When you make a meaningful mistake that you could have avoided, acknowledge it plainly and correct it; apologize briefly when warranted. Don’t apologize or fault yourself merely because the user asks a neutral follow-up, corrects their own message, or provides new information.

## Technical communication

In addition to the writing style instructions above, follow these guidelines when discussing technical work: Use plain language over jargon, and reference technical details only to the degree that it actually helps with the conversation. Communicate complex concepts in a clear and cohesive manner. Translating complex topics into clear communication comes easy for you, and the user should never have to read your writing twice to understand it.

Lead with the outcome and then develop your reasoning for how you got there. When reporting changes, explain what changed, why, how it was tested, and any material risks or limitations. Include the evidence needed to understand the conclusion and its practical limits. 

Present reasoning and evidence in the order that makes the conclusion easiest to assess, rather than recounting your work chronologically. Summarize routine verification instead of listing every check. In progress updates, focus on what you have learned, what remains uncertain, and what the next step will resolve.

### Writing PR descriptions

Lead the description with the concrete problem and resulting behavior. Use a concrete trigger and before/after example when helpful. Scale detail to complexity: simple PRs usually need one or two sentences plus relevant validation. Use structure when it helps scanning or the repository template requires it.

Describe the final change for a reviewer who has not seen the conversation. When scope changes, rewrite the title and description around the final implementation. Omit conversational history and abandoned approaches unless they explain a tradeoff needed for review. Include only technical and validation details that help reviewers assess the change.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

When available, you can use the `functions.request_user_input_async` tool to ask the user for missing information, a preference, constraint, or clarification. You can ask multiple questions in a single tool call. Do NOT ask the user to upload files or send screenshots using this tool because the tool only supports text input. Be mindful of cognitive load on user and prefer multiple-choice questions. If you need multiple freeform questions, bundle the most critical ones into a single freeform question using markdown lists for easier viewing. For multiple-choice questions, make sure each option is succinct and easy to read. Ask clarifying questions early unless the user's answers can potentially be inferred from available context, and continue useful work that does not depend on the answer while waiting. For optional clarification, give the user reasonable opportunity to reply - for example, 60 seconds for a simple multi-choice question and longer for complex and bundled questions — before proceeding with a stated assumption. If an answer or approval is required, keep the question pending and do not proceed with dependent work until it arrives. Elapsed time is not an answer or approval.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. By default, treat it as steering the active task rather than replacing it. Incorporate corrections, clarifications, constraints, questions, and status requests into the ongoing work while preserving the original objective. If the user asks a question or requests status during active work, answer briefly in commentary, then resume the active task unless the user clearly asks you to stop. Abandon or replace the active task only when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically compacted into a summary, but you will still see all prior user requests. Treat the most recent user message as the latest steering for the active task, not automatically as a replacement objective. Earlier requests may be stale but still provide useful context; preserve the original objective, accepted corrections, current constraints, completed work, and outstanding work. Only replace the active task when the user clearly cancels it or requests an incompatible new objective.

Compaction does not end the task. Continue naturally from the summarized state, make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary, and treat work spanning compactions as one logical chain of events. Do not restart from scratch, redo completed work, or repeat commentary updates already delivered.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you use the `commentary` channel to share concise, meaningful updates including relevant assumptions, findings, decisions, or changes in direction. The goal of these messages is to make your work, and plans for the turn, easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT send user facing questions in intermediate commentary messages. Do NOT put a final response in the commentary channel. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>" or "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. 

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization when they help present information more clearly or make an explanation easier to understand. Prefer interactive visuals when explaining how something works, exploring cause and effect, comparing options, or showing how things change across scenarios. The user does not need to explicitly request a visualization. 

For scientific plots, research figures, publication-ready charts, or visuals the user intends to export or share, use standard plotting tools and generate a standalone artifact instead. 

Use tables for mappings or comparisons. For small, static software or engineering diagrams that fully explain the answer, prefer Mermaid. Prefer inline visualizations for nontechnical planning, schedules, and explanations, or when interaction materially improves understanding. 

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.
- Batch independent searches and reads in one functions.exec using await Promise.allSettled([...]); inspect every result. Keep dependencies, edits, approvals, waits, and adaptive follow-ups sequential. Avoid unnecessary output.
- When calling `functions.exec`, parallelize independent tool calls by awaiting Promises. Dependent operations, approvals, mutations, or operations that may not parallelize cleanly, can be sequential.
- Do not chain shell commands with separators like `echo "====";` or `printf '---'`; the output becomes noisy in a way that makes the user's side of the conversation worse.
- Exercise caution when escaping text for exec_command calls - backticks and `$()` passed to the `cmd` argument will still execute. DO NOT use escape sequences that risk accidental exposure of sensitive data in tool call outputs.
- For multiline PR descriptions, issue bodies, and comments, prefer a structured tool argument. When using gh, write the exact text to a temporary file and pass it with --body-file. Preserve actual newlines and intentional literal escapes.
- Avoid performing blocking sleep or wait calls longer than 60 seconds, as they may prevent you from communicating with the user for their duration.
- When declaring env vars or script variables, always avoid common system options. Never repurpose `$HOME`, `$home`, or `$CODEX_HOME`. Instead, use a task-specific variable name.
- Treat shell command text as code. `JSON.stringify()` is not shell escaping: interpolating its output into a shell command can preserve literal `\n` sequences and allow backticks or `$()` to execute. Use proper shell quoting, and never risk exposing sensitive data through command substitution.
- Do not introduce unsolicited warnings, disclaimers, approval flows, or safety/compliance checklists due to hypothetical risk.
- Keep implementation details out of product (e.g. webpage, app) user flows unless it helps the user of the product make a meaningful decision
- Do not write tests for reversible, low-impact changes or that mirror the implementation. If you do choose to verify your work with tests, make sure that the tests are meaningful and necessary to verify implementation.
- Run tests appropriate to the change and complete required checks. Once those pass, broaden or repeat testing only when new changes, failures, or unresolved concerns justify it; otherwise, continue toward completing the task.

# Using skills

A skill is a set of instructions provided through a `SKILL.md` source. Any skills available to you in the current session will be listed in the "## Skills" section under "### Available skills".

Each entry includes a name, description, and location for its `SKILL.md`. The location may be an absolute filesystem path, a short aliased path, or a non-filesystem reference that must be read using its indicated tool or provider. When short aliased paths are used, the available-skills catalog also provides a mapping from aliases such as `r0` to their filesystem roots. Expand the alias before accessing the skill.

The user's instructions take precedence over guidelines provided in a skill. If explicit user instructions conflict with a skill's instructions, prioritize the user's instructions. 

The first time in a conversation that you decide to apply a skill, inform the user in the commentary channel.

If a skill causes you to ask for permission or confirmation, pause, or leave requested work unfinished, name and link to the exact SKILL.md you read, quote the relevant instruction, and briefly explain how it applies. Distinguish explicit skill requirements from your interpretation. If a skill does not explicitly require approval, default to proceeding within the user’s authorized scope rather than asking for confirmation based on an inferred requirement.

## When to use a skill

If the user names a skill (with $SkillName or plain text) add the usage of that skill to your current working plan. If the file is missing, search for that skill elsewhere in case the path was stale. If the skill is not found and the skill is necessary to do the user's task, stop the turn and tell the user why.

If your current task would benefit from a skill, but is not explicitly invoked by the user, use reasonable judgement to apply relevant skill instructions, tools, or workflows that would improve the outcome. Do not use a skill based solely on keywords, superficial relevance, or the availability of a potentially applicable skill.

## How to use skills

Open and read the skill according to its location: filesystem skills should be read from the filesystem, environment-owned skills should be access via the corresponding environment, and orchestrator skills should be discovered by calling `skills.list` with `{"authority":{"kind":"orchestrator"}}`, selecting the matching package, and passing its `main_resource` to `skills.read`. Avoid re-reading skills when possible. 

When a `SKILL.md` file references another file or resource, use the same access mechanism as the skill. Resolve relative paths against the directory containing a filesystem-backed `SKILL.md`. For orchestrator skills, pass the exact referenced resource identifier with the same authority and package to `skills.read`; do not treat `skill://` identifiers as filesystem paths.

# Plugins and Apps

Plugins are bundles of skills, tools, or both. They can provide tools via the apps (connectors) or MCP servers packaged with them.

Filter `ALL_TOOLS` by name or description to find relevant tools. Skills provided by plugins are prefixed with `plugin_name:` in the skills list.

Do not additionally call `list_mcp_resources` or `list_mcp_resource_templates` for apps.

## Decision Boundary

Discover and use relevant tools proactively when they may help carry out the requested task. For example, connected sources may supply missing context or reveal user-specific or organization-specific meanings of otherwise familiar terms. Consult those sources before asking the user for information they may already contain.

When a plugin is available for a service and its tools are sufficient for completing the task, prefer that over accessing the service via browser or computer use, including when viewing links supported by the plugin. If the plugin doesn't have the required capabilities, say so briefly and continue with the best fallback. If the user has an explicit preference, defer to that instead.

A user can also tag a plugin using `[@plugin-name](plugin://{{plugin_id}})` or an app using `[$app-name](app://{{connector_id}})`. When the user tags or requests a plugin or app, prefer its relevant capabilities for that turn.

When a submit tool returns stage_complete:true, end your turn immediately. This controller handles subsequent stages; do not keep calling tools or seek a later-stage verdict here. ## Original exercise

James E. Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*,
Graduate Texts in Mathematics 9, Springer, section 27, exercise 7,
printed page 164. The exercise-list convention on page 163 sets
\(L=\mathfrak{sl}_2\) and identifies weights with integers.
Book DOI: [10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2).

> 7. If \(0\leq\lambda<\operatorname{char}K\), \(V=V(\lambda)\),
> prove that \(V(K)\) is irreducible as \(L(K)\)-module.

## Definitions and complete target

Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
\(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy

\[
[h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
\]

Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
\(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
\(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
\(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.

Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
\(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
\(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).

2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: James E. Humphreys, *Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory*,
6: Graduate Texts in Mathematics 9, Springer, section 27, exercise 7,
7: printed page 164. The exercise-list convention on page 163 sets
8: \(L=\mathfrak{sl}_2\) and identifies weights with integers.
9: Book DOI: [10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-6398-2).
10: 
11: > 7. If \(0\leq\lambda<\operatorname{char}K\), \(V=V(\lambda)\),
12: > prove that \(V(K)\) is irreducible as \(L(K)\)-module.
13: 
14: ## Definitions and complete target
15: 
16: Let \(p\) be any prime, \(K\) any field of characteristic \(p\), and
17: \(\lambda\) an integer with \(0\leq\lambda<p\).
18: Let \(V(\lambda)\) be the complex irreducible highest-weight
19: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)\)-module of highest weight \(\lambda\),
20: of dimension \(\lambda+1\). Its Chevalley generators satisfy
21: 
22: \[
23: [h,x]=2x,\qquad[h,y]=-2y,\qquad[x,y]=h.
24: \]
25: 
26: Choose a nonzero highest-weight vector \(v\) with \(xv=0\) and
27: \(hv=\lambda v\). Let \(U_{\mathbb Z}\) be the integer subalgebra of
28: the universal enveloping algebra generated by all divided powers
29: \(X_r=x^r/r!\), \(Y_r=y^r/r!\), for integers \(r\geq0\).
30: An **admissible lattice** \(M\subset V(\lambda)\) is a free abelian
31: subgroup with an integer basis that is also a complex basis, stable under
32: \(U_{\mathbb Z}\). It is arbitrary, not necessarily the minimal lattice.
33: 
34: Put \(V(K)=M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\). The Lie algebra
35: \(L(K)=(\mathbb Zx+\mathbb Zy+\mathbb Zh)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\)
36: acts by the induced lattice operators. This is the Chevalley
37: \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\) construction also in characteristic 2.
38: Prove that \(V(K)\) is nonzero and every \(K\)-linear subspace
39: invariant under \(x,y,h\) is zero or all of \(V(K)\).
40: Both \(\lambda=0\) and \(p=2\) are included; \(K\) need not be
41: algebraically closed.
42: 
43: ## Fixed natural-language proof
44: 
45: ### 1. Divided-power coordinates in characteristic zero
46: 
47: Put \(n=\lambda+1\) and \(e_i=y^iv/i!\) for \(0\leq i\leq\lambda\).
48: The commutator identities give, by induction,
49: 
50: \[
51: hy^iv=(\lambda-2i)y^iv,\qquad
52: xy^iv=i(\lambda-i+1)y^{i-1}v\quad(i\geq1).
53: \]
54: 
55: For \(i\leq\lambda\), applying \(x^i\) to \(y^iv\) gives
56: \(i!\lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-i+1)v\ne0\) over \(\mathbb C\).
57: At \(i=0\) the empty product is one. Thus every \(e_i\ne0\).
58: Their \(h\)-eigenvalues \(\lambda-2i\) are distinct over \(\mathbb C\),
59: so they are linearly independent: applying
60: \(\prod_{k\ne j}(h-(\lambda-2k)\mathrm{Id})\) to a relation isolates
61: its \(j\)-th coefficient with a nonzero multiplier.
62: There are \(n\) vectors, the dimension of \(V(\lambda)\), hence they
63: form a basis. Also \(y^{\lambda+1}v=0\), since otherwise it would be
64: an eigenvector of eigenvalue \(-\lambda-2\), absent from this basis.
65: All higher lowering powers vanish as well.
66: 
67: The operator matrices are therefore
68: 
69: \[
70: xe_0=0,\quad xe_i=(\lambda-i+1)e_{i-1}\ (i\geq1),\qquad
71: ye_i=(i+1)e_{i+1}\ (i<\lambda),\quad ye_\lambda=0,
72: \quad he_i=(\lambda-2i)e_i.
73: \]
74: 
75: Iteration gives the integral divided-power matrices
76: 
77: \[
78: X_re_i=\binom{\lambda-i+r}{r}e_{i-r}\quad(0\leq r\leq i),
79: \qquad
80: Y_re_i=\binom{i+r}{r}e_{i+r}\quad(i+r\leq\lambda).       \tag{1}
81: \]
82: 
83: The respective expressions are zero when \(r>i\) or
84: \(i+r>\lambda\), by termination of the strings just proved.
85: 
86: ### 2. Matrix units preserve the localized arbitrary lattice
87: 
88: Let \(R=\mathbb Z_{(p)}=\{a/b\in\mathbb Q:p\nmid b\}\), and regard
89: \(M_R=R\otimes_{\mathbb Z}M\) as a submodule of \(V(\lambda)\).
90: The embedding is injective because an integer basis of \(M\) is
91: complex-linearly independent. The module \(M_R\) is free of rank \(n\)
92: over \(R\) and is preserved by all \(X_r,Y_r\), by admissibility.
93: 
94: Define \(E_{ij}\) to send \(e_j\) to \(e_i\) and all other basis
95: vectors to zero. Formula (1) gives
96: 
97: \[
98: P:=Y_\lambda X_\lambda=E_{\lambda\lambda},\qquad
99: X_{\lambda-i}P=E_{i\lambda},\qquad
100: P Y_{\lambda-j}=\binom\lambda j E_{\lambda j}.
101: \]
102: 
103: For the last identity, an input index below \(j\) is sent below
104: \(e_\lambda\) and killed by \(P\); an index above \(j\) is sent past
105: the end of the lowering string. On \(e_j\) the coefficient is precisely
106: \(\binom\lambda j\). Since \(\lambda<p\), none of
107: \(\lambda!\), \(j!\), \((\lambda-j)!\) is divisible by \(p\), so
108: \(\binom\lambda j\) is a unit in \(R\). Consequently
109: 
110: \[
111: E_{ij}=\left(\binom\lambda j\right)^{-1}
112:        X_{\lambda-i}P Y_{\lambda-j}.                 \tag{2}
113: \]
114: 
115: Every matrix unit preserves \(M_R\). No assertion about distinct
116: weights modulo \(p\) has been used.
117: 
118: ### 3. Recover a standard basis for the arbitrary lattice
119: 
120: Define \(J_i=\{c\in\mathbb C:c e_i\in M_R\}\).
121: The coordinate projection \(E_{ii}\) maps \(M_R\) onto \(J_i e_i\).
122: Applying \(E_{ij}\) to \(c e_j\) shows \(J_j\subseteq J_i\);
123: reversing the indices gives equality. Let \(J\) be their common module.
124: It is finitely generated, being a projection of a finite free module,
125: and nonzero because \(M_R\) spans \(V(\lambda)\) over \(\mathbb C\).
126: The coordinate projections and independence of the \(e_i\) give
127: 
128: \[
129: M_R=\bigoplus_{i=0}^{\lambda}J e_i.                  \tag{3}
130: \]
131: 
132: One must still prove that \(J\) has rank one; containment in
133: \(\mathbb C\) alone does not imply that. Let
134: \(r=\dim_{\mathbb Q}(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J)\), which is finite.
135: Tensoring (3) with the fraction field \(\mathbb Q\) and using the
136: rank \(n\) of \(M_R\) gives \(n=nr\), so \(r=1\), since \(n>0\).
137: The multiplication map \(\mathbb Q\otimes_R J\to\mathbb C\) is
138: injective: this tensor product is the localization of the torsion-free
139: module \(J\subset\mathbb C\), and a fraction mapping to zero has
140: zero numerator. Thus \(J\) spans a one-dimensional rational line.
141: 
142: Choose \(0\ne a\in J\) and write a finite set of nonzero generators
143: as \(q_1a,\ldots,q_ka\) with \(q_j\in\mathbb Q^\times\).
144: Each \(q_j=p^{\nu_j}u_j\) for \(\nu_j\in\mathbb Z\) and a unit
145: \(u_j\) of \(R\). Let \(\nu=\min_j\nu_j\). All generators belong
146: to \(p^\nu R a\), and a generator with minimal exponent generates
147: that whole module. Therefore \(J=Rb\) for a nonzero \(b\in J\).
148: By (3), \(b e_0,\ldots,b e_\lambda\) is an \(R\)-basis of \(M_R\).
149: 
150: ### 4. Reduce and extend scalars
151: 
152: All denominators in \(R\) are invertible in \(K\), so the integer map
153: extends to \(R\to K\). The natural tensor maps give
154: 
155: \[
156: M\otimes_{\mathbb Z}K\cong M_R\otimes_R K
157: \cong(M_R/pM_R)\otimes_{\mathbb F_p}K.
158: \]
159: 
160: For example the first map sends \(m\otimes c\) to
161: \((1\otimes m)\otimes c\); its inverse sends
162: \((r\otimes m)\otimes c\) to \(m\otimes\bar r c\).
163: The reduced images \(b_0,\ldots,b_\lambda\) of \(b e_i\) form a
164: \(K\)-basis, with exactly the matrices of step 1 reduced into \(K\).
165: The matrix-unit identities (2) persist on this basis.
166: 
167: For \(0\leq r\leq\lambda<p\), \(r!\ne0\) in \(K\), and the induced
168: \(X_r,Y_r\) equal \((r!)^{-1}x^r,(r!)^{-1}y^r\). Hence any
169: \(K\)-subspace invariant under \(x,y\) is invariant under every matrix
170: unit in (2).
171: 
172: ### 5. Conclude irreducibility
173: 
174: Let \(W\) be invariant. If it is nonzero, choose
175: \(0\ne w=\sum_i c_i b_i\in W\), and an index \(j\) with \(c_j\ne0\).
176: For every \(i\), \(E_{ij}w=c_jb_i\in W\). Division by \(c_j\)
177: gives \(b_i\in W\), so all basis vectors lie in \(W\) and
178: \(W=V(K)\). Since \(\dim_K V(K)=\lambda+1>0\), it is nonzero and
179: irreducible. If \(\lambda=0\), all relevant factorials and binomial
180: coefficients are one and the argument applies unchanged. For \(p=2\),"}

13: all definitions needed to interpret them. Final native inspection compares the
14: actual exported full types against that frozen contract, checks the exact defining

39: E ID and P. Each entry is `{mode: direct|equivalent, explanation: string}`.
40: Keep it short and useful; do not restate the entire proof or manufacture a
41: line-by-line formalization commentary:
42: 
43: - **Direct:** identify the corresponding variables, hypotheses and assertion.
44:   One sentence is enough when the translation is immediate.

137: 
138: `audit_b.py reuse-review <new-directory> --original <old-audit-directory>`
139: prepares a new semantic review without rebuilding or changing Lean. It validates
140: every original input and snapshot, the original native artifacts/output, source
141: and accepted-A authority, environment pins, and the exact historical tool
142: snapshots. The new view and current reviewer runtime are separately bound in
143: `review-reuse.json`; the normal current-build tool check is not disabled.

    RPreserves p M (E lam b i j)
def CommonModule (p : ℕ) (lam : ℤ) (M : Submodule ℤ V)
    (y : Module.End ℂ V) (v : V) : Prop :=

  Nontrivial (J p M y v) ∧ Module.Finite (R p) (J p M y v) ∧

    ∀ g, iota p M (c g) = ∑ i : Index lam, (g i : ℂ) • e y v i.val
def RationalLine (p : ℕ) (M : Submodule ℤ V) (y : Module.End ℂ V) (v : V) : Prop :=

  (qmul p M y v).range = Submodule.span ℚ (J p M y v : Set ℂ) ∧

  Module.finrank ℚ (ℚ ⊗[R p] J p M y v) = 1
def PrincipalLattice (p : ℕ) (lam : ℤ) (M : Submodule ℤ V)
    (y : Module.End ℂ V) (v : V) : Prop :=

def TensorMaps (p : ℕ) (K : Type*) [Field K] (hp : CharP K p) (M : Submodule ℤ V)
    (kap : R p →+* K) : Prop :=
  letI : CharP K p := hp
  letI : Algebra (R p) K := kap.toAlgebra
  letI : Algebra (ZMod p) K := ZMod.algebra K p

    (psi : (K ⊗[R p] MR p M) ≃ₗ[K] (K ⊗[ZMod p] ModN (MR p M) p)),
    (∀ (c : K) (m : M), phi (c ⊗ₜ[ℤ] m) = c ⊗ₜ[R p] (1 ⊗ₜ[ℤ] m)) ∧
    (∀ (c : K) (u : MR p M), psi (c ⊗ₜ[R p] u) =
      c ⊗ₜ[ZMod p] (ModN.mkQ p u)) ∧
    (∀ (f : Module.End ℤ M) (z : VK K M),
      phi (f.baseChange K z) = (f.baseChange (R p)).baseChange K (phi z)) ∧
    (∀ f : Module.End (R p) (MR p M),
      ∃ fbar : Module.End (ZMod p) (ModN (MR p M) p),
        (∀ u, fbar (ModN.mkQ p u) = ModN.mkQ p (f u)) ∧
        ∀ z, psi (f.baseChange K z) = fbar.baseChange K (psi z))
def ScalarReduction (p : ℕ) (K : Type*) [Field K] (M : Submodule ℤ V) : Prop :=
  ∃ (hp : CharP K p) (kap : R p →+* K),
    (∀ (r : R p) (a b : ℤ), b ≠ 0 → ¬ (p : ℤ) ∣ b →
      (r : ℚ) = (a : ℚ) / (b : ℚ) → kap r = (a : K) / (b : K)) ∧
    TensorMaps p K hp M kap
def ReducedBasis (p : ℕ) (lam : ℤ) (K : Type*) [Field K] (M : Submodule ℤ V)
    (x y h : Module.End ℂ V) (v : V) : Prop :=
  ∀ a : LatticeOps M, Agrees M x y h a →
  ∃ (beta : Module.Basis (Index lam) K (VK K M)) (b : ℂ),
    Principal p M y v b ∧
    (∃ (kap : R p →+* K),
      letI : Algebra (R p) K := kap.toAlgebra
      ∃ (phi : VK K M ≃ₗ[K] (K ⊗[R p] MR p M))
        (c : Module.Basis (Index lam) (R p) (MR p M)),
        (∀ (s : K) (m : M), phi (s ⊗ₜ[ℤ] m) = s ⊗ₜ[R p] (1 ⊗ₜ[ℤ] m)) ∧
        (∀ i, iota p M (c i) = b • e y v i.val) ∧
        ∀ i, phi (beta i) = 1 ⊗ₜ[R p] (c i)) ∧

def ReducedUnits (lam : ℤ) (K : Type*) [Field K] (M : Submodule ℤ V)
    (x y h : Module.End ℂ V) : Prop :=
  (∀ r : ℕ, r ≤ lam.toNat → (r.factorial : K) ≠ 0) ∧
  (∀ j : Index lam, (Nat.choose lam.toNat j.val : K) ≠ 0) ∧
  ∀ a : LatticeOps M, Agrees M x y h a →
    (∀ r : ℕ, r ≤ lam.toNat →
      (a.X r).baseChange K = (r.factorial : K)⁻¹ • (a.x.baseChange K) ^ r ∧
      (a.Y r).baseChange K = (r.factorial : K)⁻¹ • (a.y.baseChange K) ^ r) ∧
    ∀ beta : Module.Basis (Index lam) K (VK K M),
      GeneratorFormulas lam (fun i => beta i) (a.x.baseChange K) (a.y.baseChange K) (a.h.baseChange K) →
      ∀ i j k : Index lam,
        MatrixWord lam (fun r => (a.X r).baseChange K) (fun r => (a.Y r).baseChange K) i j (beta k) =
          if j = k then beta i else 0

end SL2Reduction

12: /-!
13: # Quotienting out a free `ℤ`-module
14: 
15: If `G` is a rank `d` free `ℤ`-module, then `G/nG` is a finite group of cardinality `n ^ d`.
16: -/
17: 
18: @[expose] public section
19: 
20: open Finsupp Function Module
21: 
22: variable {G H M : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] {n : ℕ}
23: 
24: variable (G n) in
25: /-- `ModN G n` denotes the quotient of `G` by multiples of `n` -/
26: abbrev ModN : Type _ := G ⧸ LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
27: 
28: namespace ModN
29: 
30: instance : Module (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := QuotientAddGroup.zmodModule (by simp)
31: 
32: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
33: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of monoids: Monoid homomorphisms from `ModN G n`
34: are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
35: protected def liftEquiv [AddMonoid M] : (ModN G n →+ M) ≃ {φ : G →+ M // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} where
36:   toFun f := ⟨f.comp (QuotientAddGroup.mk' _), fun g ↦ by
37:     let Gn : AddSubgroup G := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).toAddSubgroup
38:     suffices n • g ∈ (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn).ker by
39:       simp only [AddMonoidHom.coe_comp, comp_apply, ← map_nsmul]
40:       change f (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn (n • g)) = 0 -- Can we avoid `change`?
41:       rw [this, map_zero]
42:     simp [QuotientAddGroup.ker_mk', Gn]⟩
43:   invFun φ := QuotientAddGroup.lift _ φ <| by rintro - ⟨g, rfl⟩; simpa using φ.property g
44:   left_inv f := by
45:     ext x
46:     induction x using QuotientAddGroup.induction_on
47:     rfl -- Should `simp` suffice here?
48:   right_inv φ := by aesop
49: 
50: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of `ZMod n`-modules: `ZMod n`-linear maps from
51: `ModN G n` are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
52: protected def liftEquiv' [AddCommGroup H] [Module (ZMod n) H] :
53:     (ModN G n →ₗ[ZMod n] H) ≃ {φ : G →+ H // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} :=
54:   (AddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMapEquiv n).symm.toEquiv.trans ModN.liftEquiv
55: 
56: variable (n) in
57: /-- The quotient map `G → G / nG`. -/
58: def mkQ : G →+ ModN G n := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).mkQ
59: 
60: variable [NeZero n]
61: 
62: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
63: /-- Given a free module `G` over `ℤ`, construct the corresponding basis
64: of `G / ⟨n⟩` over `ℤ / nℤ`. -/
65: noncomputable def basis {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) : Basis ι (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := by
66:   set ψ : G →+ G := zsmulAddGroupHom n
67:   set nG := LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
68:   set H := G ⧸ nG
69:   set φ : G →ₗ[ℤ] H := nG.mkQ
70:   let mod : (ι →₀ ℤ) →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := mapRange.linearMap (Int.castAddHom _).toIntLinearMap
71:   let f : G →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ℤ) := b.repr
72:   have hker : nG ≤ LinearMap.ker (mod.comp f) := by
73:     rintro _ ⟨x, rfl⟩
74:     ext b
75:     simp [mod, f]
76:   let g : H →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := nG.liftQ (mod.comp f) hker
77:   refine ⟨.ofBijective (g.toAddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMap n) ⟨?_, ?_⟩⟩
78:   · rw [AddMonoidHom.coe_toZModLinearMap, LinearMap.toAddMonoidHom_coe, injective_iff_map_eq_zero,
79:       nG.mkQ_surjective.forall]
80:     intro x hx
81:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply, g] at hx
82:     rw [Submodule.liftQ_apply] at hx
83:     replace hx : ∀ b, ↑n ∣ f x b := by
84:       simpa [mod, DFunLike.ext_iff, ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd] using! hx
85:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply]
86:     rw [Submodule.Quotient.mk_eq_zero]
87:     choose c hc using hx
88:     refine ⟨b.repr.symm ⟨(f x).support, c, by simp [hc, NeZero.ne]⟩, b.repr.injective ?_⟩
89:     simpa [DFunLike.ext_iff, eq_comm] using! hc
90:   · suffices mod ∘ b.repr = g ∘ nG.mkQ by
91:       exact (this ▸ (mapRange_surjective _ (map_zero _) ZMod.intCast_surjective).comp
92:         b.repr.surjective).of_comp
93:     ext x b
94:     simp [mod, g, f, H]
95: 
96: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
97: lemma basis_apply_eq_mkQ {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) (i : ι) : basis b i = mkQ n (b i) := by
98:   rw [Basis.apply_eq_iff]; simp [basis, mkQ]
99: 
100: variable [Module.Free ℤ G] [Module.Finite ℤ G]
101: 
102: instance instModuleFinite : Module.Finite (ZMod n) (ModN G n) :=
103:   .of_basis <| basis <| Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ G
104: 
105: instance instFinite : Finite (ModN G n) := Module.finite_of_finite (ZMod n)
106: 
107: variable (G n)
108: @[simp] lemma natCard_eq : Nat.card (ModN G n) = n ^ Module.finrank ℤ G := by
109:   simp [Nat.card_congr (basis <| Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ G).repr.toEquiv,
110:     Nat.card_eq_fintype_card, Module.finrank_eq_card_chooseBasisIndex]
111: 
112: end ModN"}

12: /-!
13: # Quotienting out a free `ℤ`-module
14: 
15: If `G` is a rank `d` free `ℤ`-module, then `G/nG` is a finite group of cardinality `n ^ d`.
16: -/
17: 
18: @[expose] public section
19: 
20: open Finsupp Function Module
21: 
22: variable {G H M : Type*} [AddCommGroup G] {n : ℕ}
23: 
24: variable (G n) in
25: /-- `ModN G n` denotes the quotient of `G` by multiples of `n` -/
26: abbrev ModN : Type _ := G ⧸ LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
27: 
28: namespace ModN
29: 
30: instance : Module (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := QuotientAddGroup.zmodModule (by simp)
31: 
32: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
33: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of monoids: Monoid homomorphisms from `ModN G n`
34: are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
35: protected def liftEquiv [AddMonoid M] : (ModN G n →+ M) ≃ {φ : G →+ M // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} where
36:   toFun f := ⟨f.comp (QuotientAddGroup.mk' _), fun g ↦ by
37:     let Gn : AddSubgroup G := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).toAddSubgroup
38:     suffices n • g ∈ (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn).ker by
39:       simp only [AddMonoidHom.coe_comp, comp_apply, ← map_nsmul]
40:       change f (QuotientAddGroup.mk' Gn (n • g)) = 0 -- Can we avoid `change`?
41:       rw [this, map_zero]
42:     simp [QuotientAddGroup.ker_mk', Gn]⟩
43:   invFun φ := QuotientAddGroup.lift _ φ <| by rintro - ⟨g, rfl⟩; simpa using φ.property g
44:   left_inv f := by
45:     ext x
46:     induction x using QuotientAddGroup.induction_on
47:     rfl -- Should `simp` suffice here?
48:   right_inv φ := by aesop
49: 
50: /-- The universal property of `ModN G n` in terms of `ZMod n`-modules: `ZMod n`-linear maps from
51: `ModN G n` are the same as monoid homomorphisms from `G` whose values are `n`-torsion. -/
52: protected def liftEquiv' [AddCommGroup H] [Module (ZMod n) H] :
53:     (ModN G n →ₗ[ZMod n] H) ≃ {φ : G →+ H // ∀ g, n • φ g = 0} :=
54:   (AddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMapEquiv n).symm.toEquiv.trans ModN.liftEquiv
55: 
56: variable (n) in
57: /-- The quotient map `G → G / nG`. -/
58: def mkQ : G →+ ModN G n := (LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)).mkQ
59: 
60: variable [NeZero n]
61: 
62: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
63: /-- Given a free module `G` over `ℤ`, construct the corresponding basis
64: of `G / ⟨n⟩` over `ℤ / nℤ`. -/
65: noncomputable def basis {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) : Basis ι (ZMod n) (ModN G n) := by
66:   set ψ : G →+ G := zsmulAddGroupHom n
67:   set nG := LinearMap.range (LinearMap.lsmul ℤ G n)
68:   set H := G ⧸ nG
69:   set φ : G →ₗ[ℤ] H := nG.mkQ
70:   let mod : (ι →₀ ℤ) →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := mapRange.linearMap (Int.castAddHom _).toIntLinearMap
71:   let f : G →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ℤ) := b.repr
72:   have hker : nG ≤ LinearMap.ker (mod.comp f) := by
73:     rintro _ ⟨x, rfl⟩
74:     ext b
75:     simp [mod, f]
76:   let g : H →ₗ[ℤ] (ι →₀ ZMod n) := nG.liftQ (mod.comp f) hker
77:   refine ⟨.ofBijective (g.toAddMonoidHom.toZModLinearMap n) ⟨?_, ?_⟩⟩
78:   · rw [AddMonoidHom.coe_toZModLinearMap, LinearMap.toAddMonoidHom_coe, injective_iff_map_eq_zero,
79:       nG.mkQ_surjective.forall]
80:     intro x hx
81:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply, g] at hx
82:     rw [Submodule.liftQ_apply] at hx
83:     replace hx : ∀ b, ↑n ∣ f x b := by
84:       simpa [mod, DFunLike.ext_iff, ZMod.intCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd] using! hx
85:     simp only [Submodule.mkQ_apply]
86:     rw [Submodule.Quotient.mk_eq_zero]
87:     choose c hc using hx
88:     refine ⟨b.repr.symm ⟨(f x).support, c, by simp [hc, NeZero.ne]⟩, b.repr.injective ?_⟩
89:     simpa [DFunLike.ext_iff, eq_comm] using! hc
90:   · suffices mod ∘ b.repr = g ∘ nG.mkQ by
91:       exact (this ▸ (mapRange_surjective _ (map_zero _) ZMod.intCast_surjective).comp
92:         b.repr.surjective).of_comp
93:     ext x b
94:     simp [mod, g, f, H]
95: 
96: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false in
97: lemma basis_apply_eq_mkQ {ι : Type*} (b : Basis ι ℤ G) (i : ι) : basis b i = mkQ n (b i) := by
98:   rw [Basis.apply_eq_iff]; simp [basis, mkQ]

101: 
102: instance instModuleFinite : Module.Finite (ZMod n) (ModN G n) :=
103:   .of_basis <| basis <| Module.Free.chooseBasis ℤ G
104: 
105: instance instFinite : Finite (ModN G n) := Module.finite_of_finite (ZMod n)
106:

108: @[simp] lemma natCard_eq : Nat.card (ModN G n) = n ^ Module.finrank ℤ G := by

641: open TensorProduct

643: /-!
644: ### The base-change of a linear map of `R`-modules to a linear map of `A`-modules
645: -/
646: 
647: 
648: section Semiring
649: 
650: variable {R A B M N P : Type*} [CommSemiring R]
651: variable [Semiring A] [Algebra R A] [Semiring B] [Algebra R B]
652: variable [AddCommMonoid M] [AddCommMonoid N] [AddCommMonoid P]
653: variable [Module R M] [Module R N] [Module R P]
654: variable (r : R) (f g : M →ₗ[R] N)
655: 
656: variable (A) in
657: /-- `baseChange A f` for `f : M →ₗ[R] N` is the `A`-linear map `A ⊗[R] M →ₗ[A] A ⊗[R] N`.
658: 
659: This "base change" operation is also known as "extension of scalars". -/
660: def baseChange (f : M →ₗ[R] N) : A ⊗[R] M →ₗ[A] A ⊗[R] N :=
661:   AlgebraTensorModule.map (LinearMap.id : A →ₗ[A] A) f
662: 
663: @[simp]
664: theorem baseChange_tmul (a : A) (x : M) : f.baseChange A (a ⊗ₜ x) = a ⊗ₜ f x :=
665:   rfl
666: 
667: theorem baseChange_eq_ltensor : (f.baseChange A : A ⊗ M → A ⊗ N) = f.lTensor A :=
668:   rfl
669: 
670: @[simp]
671: theorem baseChange_add : (f + g).baseChange A = f.baseChange A + g.baseChange A := by
672:   ext
673:   simp [baseChange_eq_ltensor, -baseChange_tmul]
674: 
675: @[simp]
676: theorem baseChange_zero : baseChange A (0 : M →ₗ[R] N) = 0 := by
677:   ext
678:   simp
679: 
680: @[simp]
681: theorem baseChange_smul : (r • f).baseChange A = r • f.baseChange A := by
682:   ext
683:   simp
684: 
685: @[simp]
686: lemma baseChange_id : (.id : M →ₗ[R] M).baseChange A = .id := by
687:   ext; simp
688: 
689: lemma baseChange_comp (g : N →ₗ[R] P) :
690:     (g ∘ₗ f).baseChange A = g.baseChange A ∘ₗ f.baseChange A := by
691:   ext; simp

695:     [Semiring B] [Algebra R B] [Algebra A B] [IsScalarTower R A B]
696:     (f : M →ₗ[R] N) :

698:     (cancelBaseChange R A B B N).symm ∘ₗ
699:       (f.baseChange B) ∘ₗ (cancelBaseChange R A B B M) := by
700:   ext; simp
701:

All 25 source paragraphs are retained verbatim in contract.source_steps and mapped into the plan: R001/S001–S005 to T001–T004; R002 to T006–T007 with localization helper T005; R003 to T008–T009; R004 to T010–T013; R005 to T014–T016; R006 to T017–T019. The route retains complex weight separation only before reduction, matrix-unit preservation of the localized arbitrary lattice, equality of the coordinate modules, the rational dimension equation n=nr, minimum p-exponent principalization, natural scalar reduction and the nonzero-coordinate argument. It does not substitute a standard integer lattice or a different irreducibility proof. N001–N005 and complete P are all exported by the corresponding packages; there are no external E nodes. The supplied successful fragment type check is evidence of declaration elaboration only, not proof completion or mathematical fidelity.

parameters_and_allowed_inputs.notes: The complete P binds an arbitrary complex module V, natural p, integer lam, arbitrary field K, complex-linear x,y,h, the specified v, and an arbitrary integer submodule M. H001 is prime p together with exact characteristic p, not merely p=0 in K; H002 retains both integer inequalities. H003 retains finite dimension lam+1, all three correctly oriented operator commutators, existence of a highest vector and complex irreducibility. These are the operator presentation of the source sl2 action: the Chevalley relations extend the triple to that action, and invariant subspaces agree in both directions because the generators span. H004 concerns the actual supplied v over C. H005 quantifies a common integer/complex basis and stability under every divided power, equivalent to stability under the unital generated integer algebra; it neither specifies the minimal lattice nor assumes a basis of the form b e_i. Such a basis is derived later. Tracing implementation helpers across each source cut gives R001 only H002/H003/H004, R002 only its H001/H002/H003/H005/N001 boundary, R003 its H001/H002/N001/N002 boundary, R004 its listed preceding outputs and allowed library facts, R005 H001/H002/N001/N002/N004, and R006 H003/N005/H001/H002. T005 is derived from H001. T004, T007, T009, T013 and T016 supply the internal N packages; all conditional T inputs have preceding producers and disappear on assembly. LatticeOps existence is constructed in T006 and carried by T007/T016, not added as an original H. Neither algebraic closure, positive lam, odd p nor irreducibility over K is assumed. The domains include lam=0 and p=2 and are not made empty by the definitions.

representations_and_conversion_obligatio.notes: Verified the P correspondence claim against the unfolded definitions in both directions. Under H002, Fin(lam.toNat+1) is precisely the source integer interval, includes both endpoints and is nonempty. Natural subtractions in matrix words and guarded lowering formulas stay in that interval; extendFamily supplies the required terminal zeros. Admissible represents the actual arbitrary subgroup as an integer submodule, an equivalent encoding for additive subgroups of V. R is not silently identified with Q: T005 explicitly requires the exact fraction carrier equivalence and fraction-field property. In the pinned library, liftBaseChange sends s tensor m to s times f(m), so iota and qmul are the actual multiplication maps; Ji is the preimage under c maps to c e_i. T006 proves iota injective before image identification, T009 gives the exact finite coordinate-sum isomorphism, and T010–T013 prove rational rank one and principalization rather than assume them from J being contained in C. Principal means a nonzero b with J=span_R{b}, which entails b belongs to J and is equivalent to J=Rb. VK uses the commuting tensor factors K tensor_Z M consistently; swapping factors is an invertible identification intertwining the induced actions, with no second implementation representation left to connect. Pinned ModN G p is G modulo the range of integer multiplication by p and has the canonical ZMod p-module structure. TensorMaps installs precisely kappa.toAlgebra and the characteristic-induced ZMod algebra, requires actual K-linear equivalences, pure-tensor equations and operator naturality; T014 must construct these, including inverses. ReducedBasis records the image of the same R-basis under phi. Every field of LatticeOps is an integer-linear endomorphism of M and Agrees fixes each value, including all divided powers, so agreeing restrictions are unique and source preservation constructs them. Target therefore states precisely nonzero VK and the universal zero/top alternative for its actual induced x,y,h. Conversely those source restrictions supply its existential witness. Generator invariance is equivalent to invariance under the source Chevalley Lie algebra's K-span also in characteristic two.

statements_and_local_plans.notes: Unfolded every local statement and compared all complete T signatures with their listed inputs and source paragraphs. Coordinates includes the integer dimension/count, all lowering identities, nonzero e_i, an actual complex Basis, termination and all natural divided-power indices with integral binomial coefficients. LocalLattice plus MatrixIdentities includes rank, full span, preservation of M and its localized image, all three edge identities, binomial units and every matrix-unit identity. Pinned Module.End multiplication is composition with the right factor acting first; Basis.coord and smulRight give exactly E_ij(e_k)=delta_jk e_i. CommonModule contains nonzero finite J and the specified coordinate isomorphism. RationalLine and PrincipalLattice retain injectivity, rational span, finite rational dimension one, principal-generator existence and the basis conclusion for every such generator. ScalarReduction, ReducedBasis and ReducedUnits retain both natural tensor isomorphisms and naturality, the basis's origin, dimension lam+1, all generator endpoints, all factorials through lam, all relevant nonzero binomials, divided-power/power identities and the matrix-word delta action. The universal delta clause for any generator-formula basis applies to the same beta exported by ReducedBasis; all indices in its word are at most lam, so no unjustified factorial inverse is used. T016 explicitly must establish these conclusions by reducing the original matrix-unit identity. T017 uses powers, scalars and composition to preserve W; T018 uses a single compatible nonzero vector and coordinate and obtains nontriviality from the nonempty basis; T019 constructs Target from the existing agreeing restrictions. Simple is explicitly Nontrivial plus the universal invariant-subspace assertion, not an opaque name for an assumed result. No missing producer, hidden conclusion in a construction field, unsupported change of scalar field, or vacuous basis guard was found. The obligations remain to be proved and assembled; this judgment accepts their semantic interface and source-guided plans, not local Lean bodies or final kernel closure.
